answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh at once, because it is the exact phrase from the appointment letter and the pay scale, and nobody outside the service would think to use it. It signals the makers actually know the world. 'Minister Salary' feels like clickbait: it is the one thing every Singaporean already has an opinion on, and I would worry the game is just a cheap dig or a meme. I would still be curious, but I would trust the first more.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A satirical, slightly provocative game about the famous ministerial pay benchmark, probably with a punchline about whether the climb is worth it. I would expect it to be shallow on actual civil service detail and to get grades and processes wrong, with the goal being to reach the top and see the big number. It would be catchy and shareable, but I would half expect a cheap political jab.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A drier, more authentic workplace sim that rewards insider knowledge: probation, confirmation in the appointment, acting versus substantive posts, appraisals worded carefully. I would expect gentle humour about bureaucracy and a slow-burn career story rather than a rush to the top. It might be too niche for outsiders, who would not know what it means, but I would expect it to get the details right.

best_moment.what: Made Minister at 50 and listened to the stallholder on camera. It felt like a human moment in a game that is mostly about process.

worst_moment.what: The townhall years (Y34-35) offered a single option, so there was nothing to choose, and STAND kept sliding with no explanation.

answer.held_back_by: Nothing really did. The game kept me on the rails and the ceiling rose anyway. The only drag was STAND, which fell for years while the appraisals said outstanding. That mismatch was never explained.
answer.ending_fair_why: Clean file, backed the right people, took the hard ministry, so Prime Minister follows. The declassified card was the best part, because it showed the ceiling moving. I would have liked to see the party's estimate shift earlier, though.
answer.chase_next: The ending where I take the conglomerate board seat or the tea invitation early, to see what a compromised file costs and whether the ceiling falls. The clean run was too smooth to learn from.
answer.play_again_why: The early and middle years had real dilemmas, but the late game thinned into single-option screens. I would want to know it is fixed first. Maybe later, for the other endings.

tone_breaks.note: Plausible for a campaign, but an MP's polling-day walkabouts are shown as a pure personal choice. The party machinery would usually run that, so it felt thin.

answer.title_fit_why: The game is really about being confirmed and made substantive: appraisals, ceilings, files, who vouches for you. Salary is only a number on the screen. The ending card is about the ceiling, not pay.
